title: Graphics: Design, Formats, and Color
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter asks two related questions: what makes a graphic communicate the data rather than distort or dilute it, and what lower-level choices — which device it is drawn on, which file format it is saved in, which color encoding it uses — help or hurt that goal. It assumes you can already produce a basic plot in R (`plot()`, `par()`, `pie()` and similar) and asks you to think about the design decisions you make once you can. ## Principles for a good graphic A graphic earns its place when it has a **high ratio of information to space**, and when the pattern that jumps out at the viewer is the pattern you actually want to show, rather than an artifact of how the data happen to be ordered or scaled. Some concrete guidelines follow from this. - **Reorder** categories or variables if that reveals structure better than an arbitrary or alphabetical order. - **Go beyond two dimensions carefully.** Color and varying symbol or line type both work, but avoid decorating a plot with color that carries no information. Multiple panels are usually a better third dimension than either. - **Avoid 3-D graphics** unless the third dimension truly carries information — a 3-D bar chart of two variables is usually just a worse 2-D bar chart with extra ink spent hiding bars behind other bars. - **Use small multiples.** A grid of panels sharing the same axes and scale — called a *trellis* plot in the older statistical-graphics literature — lets the eye compare panels directly, because everything except the variable of interest is held fixed. - **Choose the baseline deliberately.** Zero is usually the right baseline for a bar or area encoding. The classic trap is the stacked bar plot: once a second category sits *on top of* the first, comparing its length across two bars means comparing two intervals whose lower endpoint moves, rather than two bars that both start from a common line — and that is measurably harder to do by eye than reading off two heights against a shared zero. - **Do not encode magnitude as area, volume, or angle** where you could instead encode it as position or length. Studies of graphical perception find people are comparatively poor at judging areas, volumes, and angles, and comparatively good at judging position along a common scale — horizontal position slightly better than vertical. This is the core argument against pie charts, and it is worth keeping in mind whenever a pie-chart infographic (of the kind discussed in the exercises below) circulates online. - **Label axes and include units**, keep the ranges of axes consistent across panels meant to be compared, and use a legend where the plot needs one to be read. - **Handle overplotting.** Jitter points so that coincident values remain visible; if there are too many points for jittering to help, see the strategies under *Overplotting* below. - **Prefer vector file formats** — PDF or PostScript/EPS — over raster formats such as JPEG, PNG, or TIFF, for the reason developed in the next section. Rob Hyndman keeps a longer list of twenty rules along the same lines, and a fuller set of guidelines appears in the article on graphics typology cited in Sources. ## Devices and file formats ### Devices A plot is drawn onto a *device*. In the days of low-resolution, monochrome monitors this meant an actual piece of hardware; today it is just the context a plot is rendered into — a window on screen, or a file in some format. In a Unix environment the on-screen device is typically X11, a graphics window managed by the X11 windowing system; other platforms hand this off to their own window manager. Whichever device you print to, going from a plot developed on screen to one printed to a file usually takes iteration: the aspect ratio (width to height), the margins relative to the size of the plotting region, and the size of symbols and text relative to the whole plot can all look quite different once fixed to a particular file size, even though they looked fine in the interactive window. ### Vector vs. raster formats A *vectorized* format such as PDF represents the elements of an image — points, text, symbols, line segments — as symbolic objects, so that when the image is resized those elements rescale without any loss of resolution. A *rasterized* format such as JPEG, PNG, or TIFF instead stores individual pixels; enlarging the image only shows more of the pixels you already had, so it loses apparent resolution rather than gaining detail. Vector formats are the right default for most statistical graphics for exactly this reason. The one real downside is that a vector image with a very large number of points or line segments — each stored as its own symbolic object — can produce a large file, in which case a rasterized format is a more reasonable trade-off. Two-dimensional image plots (heatmaps, spatial fields) also make some inherent sense as raster, though anything else on the same figure, such as text, gets rasterized along with it. ### Converting between formats Unix has a range of command-line utilities for moving between formats (Windows and macOS have GUI equivalents). `pdftops` converts PDF to PostScript, and with the `-eps` flag to encapsulated PostScript; `ps2epsi` produces encapsulated PostScript directly. `gs` (Ghostscript) handles a wide range of manipulations of PostScript and PDF files, including conversion to raster formats and merging or splitting the pages of a PDF: ```bash # convert from pdf to jpeg gs -dNOPAUSE -r[xres]x[yres] -sDEVICE=jpeg -sOutputFile=file.jpg file.pdf # extract pages from a pdf gs -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET -dBATCH -dFirstPage=m \ -dLastPage=n -sOutputFile=out.pdf in.pdf # merge pdf files into one pdf gs -dNOPAUSE -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -sOUTPUTFILE=out.pdf \ -dBATCH in1.pdf in2.pdf in3.pdf ``` ## Color ### Colorspaces: RGB, HSV, HCL Color lives in a three-dimensional space, and there is more than one way to parameterize it. The default palette R uses for `col = i` is given by `palette()`, and it can be replaced with a vector of named colors (`colors()` lists the names available). The most familiar parameterization is **RGB** — the intensity of red, green, and blue, each on a scale of $[0,1]$ (or, equivalently, on the integer scale $\{0, \dots, 255\}$): ```r rgb(0.5, 0.75, 0) # each number on the scale [0, 1] col2rgb("yellowgreen") # the reverse, on the scale {0, ..., 255} ``` `rgb()` returns a hexadecimal string of the form `#RRGGBB`, where each of `RR`, `GG`, `BB` is a two-digit base-16 number from `00` to `FF` (0 to 255) — so pure red is `#FF0000`. This hex form is the one you will keep running into wherever colors are specified as strings. **HSV** — hue, saturation (a colorfulness metric), and value (brightness) — is a second parameterization. `rainbow()` varies hue while holding saturation and value fixed: ```r n <- 16 pie(rep(1, n), col = rainbow(n, s = .5)) # reduced saturation pie(rep(1, n), col = rainbow(n, v = .75)) # reduced brightness ``` **HCL** — hue, chroma, and luminance — uses a more absolute measure of colorfulness than HSV's saturation. The practical difference shows up directly: an HSV-based rainbow (via `rainbow()`) has some hues that visually "pop" more than others at the same nominal saturation and value, while an HCL-based rainbow, with chroma and luminance held fixed, does not: ```r library(colorspace) pie(rep(1, n), col = rainbow_hcl(n, c = 70, l = 70), main = 'HCL') pie(rep(1, n), col = rainbow(n), main = 'RGB') ``` The `colorspace` package builds on this to provide palettes for qualitative, sequential, and diverging data, usable directly with `ggplot2` and `shiny`. ### Choosing a color sequence Encoding a continuous variable in color requires a sequence that the eye reads as varying smoothly and, ideally, monotonically. R offers several built-in choices — `rainbow()`, `heat.colors()`, `terrain.colors()`, `topo.colors()` — and the `fields` package adds `tim.colors()`. The main failure mode to avoid is a sequence where the perceived ordering of colors does not match the ordering of the values it encodes. A useful custom construction is a **diverging** scheme, which uses two hues — one per direction — to emphasize magnitude around a central point: ```r temp.colors <- function(n = 25) { m <- floor(n / 2) blues <- hsv(h = .65, s = seq(1, 0, length = m + 1)[1:m]) reds <- hsv(h = 0, s = seq(1, 0, length = m + 1)[1:m]) c(blues, if (n %% 2 != 0) "#FFFFFF", reds[m:1]) } image.plot(1:n, 1:n, z, col = temp.colors(33), zlim = c(-3.5, 3.5)) ``` Two details make this work: `zlim` is forced symmetric about zero, and an odd number of levels (33) is used, so that the exact midpoint of the sequence — white — lands on zero. For choosing colors by hand rather than generating a sequence, the `RColorBrewer` package (backed by the ColorBrewer project) gives palettes designed separately for unordered (qualitative), sequential, and two-way diverging data. ### Overplotting many points A scatterplot with many points overlapping is both hard to read and, if saved as a vector format, liable to produce a large file (since every point is a separate symbolic object). Three strategies address this. `smoothScatter()` produces a two-dimensional density estimate with outlying individual points still shown; the `hexbin` package produces an empirical two-dimensional density by binning into hexagonal cells; and making point color partly transparent lets overplotted points show through as darker, though not every device supports this. Transparency is set as a fourth number in `rgb()`, on a scale of 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (opaque, the default), or as a fourth hexadecimal byte on the scale `00` to `FF` — `#FF000080` is half-transparent red, since `80` is half of `FF` in base 16. ```r x <- rnorm(10000); y <- rnorm(10000) plot(x, y) # naive: badly overplotted smoothScatter(x, y) # 2-d density with outliers shown plot(x, y, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .1), pch = 16, cex = .5) # transparency bin <- hexbin(x, y); plot(bin) # hexagonal binning ``` ### Colorblindness Roughly 7–8% of men are color blind, and the usual consequence is difficulty distinguishing red from green — so a color scheme built from both is a scheme a meaningful fraction of any audience cannot read correctly. The `dichromat` package's `dichromat()` function simulates the effect of colorblindness on an existing set of colors, which makes it possible to check a palette before using it: ```r library(dichromat) showpal <- function(colors) plot(seq_along(colors), rep(1, length(colors)), col = colors, pch = 16, cex = 4) showpal(palette()) # default palette under ordinary vision showpal(dichromat(palette())) # the same palette as seen with red-green colorblindness ``` Checked this way, `fields::tim.colors()` holds up reasonably well under simulated colorblindness, which is one reason to reach for it for spatial or image plots. ## Exercises The course poses several graphics for critique rather than for calculation; none has a single correct answer, and the point is to apply the principles above to a real example. 1. A [pie chart](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/blob/035a19ebd7ab88cffca907cade6d40212d575a1f/units/graphics_files/trafficking.jpeg) circulating online is intended to raise awareness of human trafficking. What do you like or dislike about how it presents its data? 2. Compare four graphics of categorical data over time: a [New York Times piece on overdose deaths](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/09/27/opinion/fentanyl-overdose-deaths.html), a [FlowingData graphic on causes of death by age and sex](https://flowingdata.com/2016/01/05/causes-of-death), a [New York Times piece on US electricity generation by source](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/08/02/climate/electricity-generation-us-states.html), and a [New York Times piece on Olympic medal history](http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/08/08/sports/olympics/history-olympic-dominance-charts.html). What approach does each take, and what do you like or dislike about each? 3. A [scatterplot of life-expectancy statistics](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/figure/81018073/dyr146f2.gif) accompanies [a paper on variation in lifespan across European countries](https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/40/6/1703/801755) in the *International Journal of Epidemiology*. What can you learn from this presentation of the data, and what alternative way of plotting it would show the patterns more clearly? (The underlying data are available as a CSV alongside the course's own exploratory plotting code, linked in Sources.) 4. Critique [this online graphic](https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/blob/035a19ebd7ab88cffca907cade6d40212d575a1f/units/graphics_files/exampleGraphic.png): what could be improved, and what works well as it stands? 5. The course materials include an example of an especially convoluted pie chart, from a New York Times advertisement from December 2014 — read it and assess what specifically goes wrong. 6. The course materials also include an older article (Wainer, 1984) cataloguing common graphical mistakes. Are the same mistakes still visible in more modern-looking graphics? 7. The course materials include a modern reinterpretation, by Gelman and Unwin, of a famous graphic by Florence Nightingale on causes of death in the British Army during the Crimean War in the 1850s. What does the reinterpretation change, and why? 8. A blog post walks through improving a real visualization of 2020-vs-2021 streaming-service market share. What was wrong with the original, and which of the principles above does each revision address? ## Sources - Berkeley STAT 243, `fall-2025/units/unit12-graphics.qmd`, sections 1 ("Good practices for graphics"), 3 ("Graphics file formats"), and 4 ("Colors") — the primary source for this chapter, used because it is the most recently updated version of this unit (its worked examples cite 2024 New York Times pieces). Converted markdown at `docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/fall-2025/units/unit12-graphics/01-1-good-practices-for-graphics.md`, `02-3-graphics-file-formats.md`, and `03-4-colors.md`. - The `fall-2024` version of the same unit (`docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/fall-2024/units/unit12-graphics/`, files `01`, `02`, `03`) is essentially identical prose and code to the fall-2025 version, with slightly older example links; it was read for comparison but nothing in this chapter is drawn from it that isn't also in fall-2025. - Two files listed alongside these, `docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/stat243-fall-2021/units/unit12-integ/01-1-differentiation.md` and `02-2-integration-optional.md`, were supplied as inputs but cover numerical differentiation and quadrature — an unrelated topic that happens to share the unit number "12" in that year's syllabus, rather than graphics. Nothing from them appears in this chapter. - Named but not supplied as source material, and not read for this chapter: the `shell.md` (2014 NY Times pie-chart advertisement), `wainer1984.md`, and `gelmanUnwin2013/index.md` items in the unit's `graphics_files` directory, and the `life_exp.csv` / `life_exp.R` exploratory-plotting files — all referenced in the course materials as example graphics for the exercises above. Also named but not supplied: Rob Hyndman's list of twenty rules for good graphics (`robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/graphics`) and the graphics-typology article cited in the course references (`doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2014.989324`).
